topics: Solid Shapes in Buildings
Every building and object is made of solid (3D) shapes
Prisms and Pyramids
A prism has two same faces at the ends joined by rectangles
Faces, Edges and Corners
Every solid has faces (F), edges (E) and corners (V)
Nets of Solid Shapes
A net is a solid opened out and flattened
Working with Cubes
A cube has 6 faces: each face shares an edge with 4 faces and is opposite to 1 face
Sorting 3D Shapes
Solid shapes can be sorted by a rule about their faces or edges
When Lines Meet
When two lines meet at a point they make an angle
Right Angles
A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a book
Acute and Obtuse Angles
Compare any angle with a right angle: less than a right angle is acute, more than a right angle is obtuse
Shapes with Straws
A straw triangle keeps its shape when pushed — it is rigid
Sides and Angles of 2D Shapes
A flat shape with straight sides has as many angles as sides
Circle: Centre, Radius and Diameter
Every point of a circle is at the same distance from its centre
Puzzling Shapes
Shapes can be cut into smaller shapes and joined into bigger ones

items: Every building and object is made of solid (3D) shapes. To model a building, look at each part (roof, pillar, base) and choose the solid shape that looks like it.
Look at each part, then choose the shape that looks like it
Removing one piece can make the model fall or stop looking like the building (pillars hold up the top)
A prism has two same faces at the ends joined by rectangles. A pyramid has one base and triangular faces that all meet at one point.
Prism → name it by the two end faces
Pyramid → name it by the base
Pyramid triangles meet at ONE point
Every solid has faces (F), edges (E) and corners (V). In a straw model the straws are the edges and the clay balls are the corners. For prisms and pyramids F + V − E = 2.
F + V − E = 2 for the prisms and pyramids of the table
Straws = edges, clay balls = corners
Prism: corners 2 × n, edges 3 × n · Pyramid: corners n + 1, edges 2 × n (n = sides of the end / base) (added)
A net is a solid opened out and flattened. It has one flat piece for every face; folding along the dotted lines gives the solid back.
Pieces in the net = faces of the solid
Same shapes as the faces, in the right places
A cube has 6 faces: each face shares an edge with 4 faces and is opposite to 1 face. Cubes can be stacked into towers and drawn on triangular dot paper.
On a die opposite faces add to 7
Two faces seen together are never opposite
If two colours are left, colour a paper cube from the views to decide
Solid shapes can be sorted by a rule about their faces or edges. When a shape fits both rules it goes in the overlap of the two circles.
Read the rule, check each shape, use the overlap for 'both'

When two lines meet at a point they make an angle. Angles are everywhere: corners of shapes, yoga postures, scissors, a hanger.
Look for the point where two lines meet
Mark each angle with a small curve
A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a book. Fold a paper twice to make a right angle checker and test any corner with it.
Right angle = square corner
Always check with the checker
Compare any angle with a right angle: less than a right angle is acute, more than a right angle is obtuse.
Acute < right < obtuse
Hold the checker on the corner to decide
A straw triangle keeps its shape when pushed — it is rigid. A rectangle, square or pentagon tilts when pushed: its sides stay the same but its angles change.
Triangle = rigid
Rectangle/square/pentagon push over: same sides, new angles
A flat shape with straight sides has as many angles as sides. A rectangle and a square have only right angles (4); other 4-sided shapes do not.
Sides = angles
Square and rectangle have only right angles
Every point of a circle is at the same distance from its centre. The radius goes from the centre to the border; the diameter goes from border to border through the centre and is double the radius.
Diameter = 2 × radius
All radii of a circle are equal; all diameters are equal
Shapes can be cut into smaller shapes and joined into bigger ones. When shapes share a side, count carefully: small ones first, then bigger ones made of them.
Count small first, then bigger shapes
One shared stick = a side of two shapes

items: What we can see depends on where we are. From high up we see more; from the ground a wall or a roof edge can hide a child, and someone up high is found only by looking up.
Where you stand decides what you see
From the top you see more
Walls and roof edges hide things; look up to find someone high

One object has many views
Top view: from above · Front view: from the front · Side view: from the side · Back view: from behind

notes.h: Rows and Columns in a Grid

Row = across · Column = up and down
Name the row and the column to find one box

notes.h: Paths and Steps on a Grid
items: On a grid we move one box at a time — right, left, up or down, never slanting. Counting the steps tells how far a thing is; fewer steps means nearer.
Move right, left, up, down — one box per step
Steps = steps across + steps up or down
Fewer steps = nearer

A drone sees the school from the top. A sight map is a drawing of a place from the top that shows where things are and the paths between them; we use it to trace routes, find the shortest way and give directions.
A sight map is a top view of a place
Trace routes with colour pencils
Compare the lengths of the traced routes
Give directions with left, right, straight and the places you pass
